name: Data Structures and Algorithms with the C++ STL: std::vector reserve() preallocation
baseline: std::vector<int> filled by push_back without reserve()
workload: 100,000 push_back calls of an int into a std::vector<int>, timed once with std::chrono::high_resolution_clock, first on a fresh vector and then on a fresh vector after reserve(100000).
claimed_speedup: Book sample output (relayed via the seed lead from the book, not shown on any repo page I opened): 0.01195 s without reserve against 0.003685 s with reserve; the book says reserve was more than 3x faster. About 3.2x (derived from the relayed numbers).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the book run. The repo root CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 23, defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to Debug when none is given and adds only -Wall -fPIC for GCC and Clang (/MP /permissive- for MSVC); no optimisation flag is set anywhere.
stars_or_usage: 63 stars; Packt companion repository of the book Data Structures and Algorithms with the C++ STL (2024)
tradeoffs: reserve() needs the final element count (or a good upper bound) up front; over-reserving wastes memory, and the gain is limited to avoiding reallocation and element moves during growth. It is a standard std::vector usage idiom, not a library.
caveats: The timings are the book's own single run (the repo holds the source, no result files), so the numbers could not be checked against a page. Absolute times of about 120 ns and 37 ns per push_back are far slower than an optimised build normally gives for int push_back, and the repo's CMake default build type is Debug with no -O flag, so the run was most likely unoptimised; an unoptimised build inflates the call overhead of push_back on both sides and the ratio in an optimised build can differ (not measured here). One run, no repetitions, compiler, flags and CPU not stated; the two loops run back to back in one process, the second on freshly allocated memory. Tier C: first-party, methodology incomplete. Files opened: chapter03/03_reserve.cpp, root CMakeLists.txt, README.md.

name: Extreme C: cache-friendly row-major matrix summation (chapter 5, example 5.6)
baseline: column-major (cache-unfriendly) traversal of the same row-major int matrix
workload: Sum of a 20,000 x 20,000 int matrix (1.6 GB, malloc'd flat array) walked in memory order (friendly-sum) against walked column by column (not-friendly-sum); timed with the shell time command, so the matrix allocation and fill are included.
claimed_speedup: Book run (relayed via the seed lead from the book, not shown on any repo page I opened): about 5.2 s row-major against about 15.4 s column-major, a gap the book puts at about 10 seconds. About 3.0x (derived from the relayed numbers).
compiler_and_flags: Book run reported as built with clang on macOS, no optimisation flags stated (relayed via lead). The repo's ch05-stack-and-heap/CMakeLists.txt sets no flags or build type (a typo'd CMAKE_EXPORT_5OMPILE_COMMANDS line and add_executable only).
stars_or_usage: 411 stars; Packt companion repository of the book Extreme C (2019)
tradeoffs: Loop order only: both versions run the same additions over the same flat array; the friendly one follows memory order. A teaching example of cache locality, not a library; applicable to any row-major buffer.
caveats: Single run each, timed by the shell around the whole program, so it includes malloc of 1.6 GB and the fill pass; compiler flags and CPU not stated and the repo carries no result files. The program accumulates into a signed int, which overflows at this size (about 4e12 expected) and is undefined behaviour in C, though both loops do the same arithmetic. The build is probably unoptimised (no flags in the repo), where the gap is dominated by cache and TLB misses and can differ when a compiler interchanges loops. The usage message in main() has a printf format bug that does not affect the timing. Tier C: first-party book measurement. Files opened: ch05-stack-and-heap/ExtremeC_examples_chapter5_6.c and CMakeLists.txt, root CMakeLists.txt and README.md.

name: GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA: CUDA prime-number range test kernel (chapter 4)
baseline: single-threaded CPU trial-division prime test (plain C++ loop over odd numbers)
workload: Trial-division primality test of every odd number from 100,001 up to 190,001 (45,001 numbers): one CUDA thread per number against a single-threaded CPU loop; the GPU side is timed with CUDA events around the kernel launch, the CPU side with std::chrono, one run.
claimed_speedup: Book output (relayed via the seed lead from the book, not shown on any repo page I opened): speedup grows with range size, 1.23x, 9.66x and 67.91x for three ranges; for the largest, CPU 15.6056 ms against GPU 0.2298 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the book run. ch4/1_primes/CMakeLists.txt has only project(primes_gpu CUDA) and add_executable, no flags and no build type, so the host loop is built unoptimised unless the reader passes a build type. Repo README lists g++ 9.4, CUDA Toolkit 12 and CMake 3.16 as the environment but no flags.
hardware: Intel Core i7-10750H and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060, per the book (relayed via lead; no hardware is listed on a repo page)
stars_or_usage: 117 stars; Packt companion repository of the book GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA (2025)
tradeoffs: Needs an NVIDIA GPU and the CUDA toolkit; kernel launch and data movement costs matter for small ranges. Embarrassingly parallel per-number work, so the gain scales with the number of candidates.
caveats: Likely invalid as a throughput measurement. By reading the source (not compiled or run here, no CUDA toolchain available): checkPrimeKernel keeps its result in a local bool isPrime that is never written to memory (the printf that would use it is commented out), so the trial-division loop has no observable effect and nvcc may delete it; the reported GPU time of 0.2298 ms for the largest range would then be mostly launch overhead, and the speedup rising roughly in step with range size (1.23x, 9.66x, 67.91x) is what a near-constant GPU time against a linear CPU time would give. The CPU result of checkPrimeCpu is also discarded and the host loop is probably unoptimised (no flags). Nothing checks that GPU and CPU results agree. The three ranges were presumably produced by editing the 'end' constant (the repo holds only the 190,001 version); no memory transfers are involved. Capped at C: speedup above 50x with unstated flags, first-party. Files opened: ch4/1_primes/primes.cu and CMakeLists.txt, ch4/readme.md.

name: GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA: CUDA vector addition kernel (chapter 4)
baseline: scalar CPU for-loop vector add (C[i] = A[i] + B[i], std::transform-equivalent)
workload: Element-wise addition of two float vectors, 10 thousand up to 100 million elements: CUDA kernel (1024 threads per block) against a single-threaded CPU loop; the repo's vector_add.cu uses N = 100,000,000 and reports kernel-only and with-copy speedups, GPU timed with CUDA events and CPU with std::chrono, one run.
claimed_speedup: Book tables (relayed via the seed lead from the book, not shown on any repo page I opened): kernel-only speedup reaches 44.04x at 100M elements; including host-to-device and device-to-host copies it falls to 1.02x (212.297 ms GPU against 218.270 ms CPU).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the book run. ch4/2_vector_add/CMakeLists.txt has only project(vector_add CUDA) and add_executable, no flags and no build type. Repo README lists g++ 9.4, CUDA Toolkit 12 and CMake 3.16 as the environment but no flags.
hardware: Intel Core i7-10750H and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060, per the book (relayed via lead; no hardware is listed on a repo page)
stars_or_usage: 117 stars; Packt companion repository of the book GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA (2025)
tradeoffs: Memory-bandwidth-bound kernel: the end-to-end win disappears once PCIe copies are counted, so it pays only when data stays resident on the device or the work per byte is larger. Needs an NVIDIA GPU and CUDA toolkit.
caveats: The headline 44x is kernel-only and excludes the two copies, which the same program shows cost almost all of the time (end-to-end 1.02x, i.e. no net gain). The CPU baseline is one scalar loop on one core built with no flags in the repo (probably unoptimised), not std::transform with a parallel policy or a vectorised loop, so the baseline is weak. Single run, no repetitions or warm-up of the kernel (first launch may include initialisation), numbers are the book's and not on a repo page, compiler flags and the CPU/GPU models come only from the book. Tier C: first-party. Files opened: ch4/2_vector_add/vector_add.cu and CMakeLists.txt.

name: GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA: shared-memory tiled matrix multiply with unroll and fmaf (chapter 7)
baseline: naive one-thread-per-element CUDA matrix multiply kernel (no cuBLAS comparison)
workload: Single-precision 2000 x 2000 matrix multiply (N = 2000, 16 x 16 tiles) on the GPU: matrixMulKernel (shared-memory tiles, #pragma unroll, fmaf) against matrixMulKernel_naive, with the plain tiled matrixMulKernel_shared also in the file; kernel time from Nsight Compute in the book's Release build.
claimed_speedup: Book (relayed via the seed lead from the book, not shown on any repo page I opened): Release kernel time fell from 47.33 ms (naive) to 33.37 ms (all optimisations), which the book calls about a 42% improvement; about 1.42x (derived from the relayed numbers).
compiler_and_flags: ch7/CMakeLists.txt: Release uses CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE -O3 and CMAKE_CUDA_FLAGS_RELEASE '-O3 -arch=sm_75 -rdc=false'; Debug uses '-g -O0 -Wall' and CUDA '-G -g -O0'. The book's headline figures are the Release ones. Repo README lists g++ 9.4, CUDA Toolkit 12 and CMake 3.16 as the environment but no flags.
hardware: Intel Core i7-10750H and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060, per the book (relayed via lead; no hardware is listed on a repo page), profiled with Nsight Compute 2023.3 (per the repo README requirements)
stars_or_usage: 117 stars; Packt companion repository of the book GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA (2025)
tradeoffs: Standard CUDA optimisation ladder (shared-memory tiling, loop unroll, fused multiply-add); fmaf changes rounding slightly so results are checked against the CPU with a 1e-4 tolerance. Needs an NVIDIA GPU, sm_75 target in the CMake file.
caveats: The baseline is the book's own naive kernel, not cuBLAS or any library: 2000^3 x 2 FLOP in 33.37 ms is about 0.48 TFLOP/s (derived), so the 'optimised' kernel is far from what a tuned library would reach on the same card. The repo's main() launches only matrixMulKernel and the other kernels are swapped in by editing the file; the 47.33 and 33.37 ms figures come from the book's profiler runs (one run per version) and are not in any repo file. The 42% figure compares times as 47.33/33.37 (speed gain), not as a reduction in time (about 29%). Debug-mode runs were slower and are not the headline. Tier C: first-party, hardware named only in the book. Files opened: ch7/matrix_multiply_float.cu, CMakeLists.txt, readme.md.

name: GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA: two-stream chunked copy and compute overlap for vector-matrix multiply (chapter 8)
baseline: same CUDA vector-matrix multiply without streams (one blocking copy of the whole matrix, then one kernel, then one copy back)
workload: Float matrix times vector for 16,380 x 16,380 and 32,760 x 32,760 matrices: matrix split into row chunks (273 to 16,380 rows) copied with cudaMemcpyAsync on two alternating streams so copy and kernel overlap, against vec_mat_mul_nostreams.cu; end-to-end GPU time with CUDA events, copies included.
claimed_speedup: Book Table 8.1 (relayed via the seed lead from the book, not shown on any repo page I opened): 25 to 31% lower execution time with streams; best 27.05% (87.03 ms) at 1020 MB and 31.37% (343.555 ms) at 4092 MB, averages of ten runs, chunks near 100-200 MB. The repo's commented-out average() calls hold the no-streams reference times 119.299 ms (16,380 matrix) and 500.615 ms (32,760 matrix); 87.03 against 119.299 and 343.555 against 500.615 reproduce the 27.05% and 31.37% (derived from page data plus the relayed averages).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. ch8/3_multiplying_with_streams/CMakeLists.txt adds the two executables with no flags and no build type. Repo README lists g++ 9.4, CUDA Toolkit 12 and CMake 3.16 as the environment but no flags.
hardware: Intel Core i7-10750H and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060, per the book (relayed via lead; no hardware is listed on a repo page); PCIe transfer rate measured near 12 GB/s per the book
stars_or_usage: 117 stars; Packt companion repository of the book GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA (2025)
tradeoffs: Needs pinned host memory, a chunk size tuned to the PCIe bandwidth and kernel speed, and extra device buffers; the matrix-vector kernel is bandwidth-bound so most of the saving is hidden transfer time. NVIDIA GPU and CUDA toolkit required.
caveats: The two programs differ in more than streams: the baseline allocates the matrix with malloc (pageable memory) while the streams version uses cudaMallocHost (pinned memory), so part of the gain is faster pinned-memory transfers rather than overlap; the repo does not isolate the two effects (no pinned, no-stream variant). The no-streams reference times in the comments are single values from the author's machine and the book's ten-run averages are not stored in the repo. The CPU run in compute() is skipped in the averaging path. Timing includes the result copy back and the stream synchronisation. Tier C: first-party, hardware from the book only. Files opened: ch8/3_multiplying_with_streams/vec_mat_mul_streams.cu, vec_mat_mul_nostreams.cu, CMakeLists.txt, ch8/readme.md.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: virtual function call instead of dynamic_cast (chapter 1)
baseline: dynamic_cast<Derived*> on a base-class pointer (type test to select behaviour)
workload: Google Benchmark, 64 repeated operations per iteration on a one-level Base/Derived hierarchy: p->f() through a virtual function against dynamic_cast<Derived*>(p) with the result kept alive by DoNotOptimize.
claimed_speedup: Book (relayed via the seed lead from the book, not shown on any repo page I opened): about 1 ns for the virtual call against 5 to 10 ns for the dynamic_cast, absolute numbers hardware dependent; about 5x to 10x (derived from the relayed numbers).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. No build line in the opened source file and the README lists no flags.
stars_or_usage: 137 stars; Packt companion repository of the book Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023)
tradeoffs: Moves the type-dependent behaviour into a virtual member (or a type tag), which needs the base class to know the operation; dynamic_cast stays the tool when the hierarchy cannot be changed.
caveats: The two benchmarks do different jobs (a call that does work against a successful type test), so the ratio compares idioms, not a drop-in replacement. The cast is the cheapest case for dynamic_cast: a one-level hierarchy where the cast always succeeds (p is Derived unless rand() returns 0); cost grows with deep or multiple inheritance and failing casts. The virtual call result is not passed to DoNotOptimize. Numbers are the book's, compiler, flags and CPU not stated, first-party. Tier C. File opened: Chapter01/02_dynamic_cast.C.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: local-buffer type-erased Function
workload: Google Benchmark of invoking a callable with four int arguments: the book's Function class (inline 16-byte buffer plus a function-pointer executor) against std::function holding the same value-capturing lambda, with a direct lambda call as floor; result kept alive with DoNotOptimize and ClobberMemory.
claimed_speedup: Book (relayed via the seed lead from the book, not shown on any repo page I opened): about 0.884 ns per call for Function against 1.33 ns for std::function; a direct lambda call takes 0.219 ns. About 1.5x (derived from the relayed numbers).
compiler_and_flags: The book's example build line is -g -O3 --std=c++20 with g++-11 or clang++ (relayed via lead); the opened source file has no build line (it needs C++20: it uses a requires clause) and the README lists no flags.
stars_or_usage: 137 stars; Packt companion repository of the book Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023)
tradeoffs: Function only accepts trivially copyable and trivially destructible callables that fit the inline buffer (two pointers by default, enforced with static_assert), so there is no heap fallback, no move-only callables and no non-trivial captures; storage is a char array accessed through reinterpret_cast; an empty Function throws std::bad_function_call when invoked.
caveats: Narrower than std::function (restricted callable types, no allocation fallback, no target() or copy semantics for non-trivial callables), so the comparison is not feature-equal. First-party author numbers: compiler, CPU and run counts not stated in the repo. The file has several variants (BM_invoke_* calls through an invoke helper; BM_lambda, BM_fast_lambda and BM_std_lambda call directly) and the data I have does not say which rows the book's three figures correspond to. Tier C. File opened: Chapter06/09_function.C (benchmarks BM_invoke_fast_function, BM_invoke_std_function, BM_invoke_lambda).

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: type-erased smart pointer with local-buffer deleter (smartptr_te_static / smartptr_te_vtable)
baseline: std::shared_ptr<int> with a custom deleter (and std::make_shared<int>)
workload: Google Benchmark, construct and destroy one smart pointer to a new int(0) allocated in a separate translation unit: the book's smartptr_te_static and smartptr_te_vtable (deleter stored inline, no control-block allocation) against std::shared_ptr with a custom deleter and make_shared; raw pointer and std::unique_ptr with a deleter as floor.
claimed_speedup: Book (relayed via the seed lead from the book, not shown on any repo page I opened): about 9.58 ns (static-function variant) and 10.4 ns (vtable variant) against 22.9 ns for std::shared_ptr with a custom deleter and 17.5 ns for make_shared; raw pointer 8.72 ns and unique_ptr 8.82 ns as floor. About 2.4x and 2.2x against shared_ptr-with-deleter (derived from the relayed numbers).
compiler_and_flags: The book's sample build line is -g -O3 --std=c++20 with whole-program optimisation off (relayed via lead); the opened sources (07_smartptr.C, 07_smartptr.h, 07_smartptr_ext.C) carry no build line and the README lists no flags.
stars_or_usage: 137 stars; Packt companion repository of the book Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023)
tradeoffs: Single-owner, move-only pointer with a type-erased deleter stored inline; no reference counting and no weak pointers. The static variant stores a function pointer plus the deleter object in a small buffer, the vtable variant a pointer to a constexpr vtable.
caveats: Not feature-equal: std::shared_ptr allocates a control block and does atomic reference counting, while the book's pointer has unique ownership; the like-for-like baseline (std::unique_ptr with a type-erased deleter, for example std::function) is not in the benchmark. Net overhead over the raw-pointer floor is only about 0.9 to 1.7 ns, so the gap is mostly the shared_ptr control block allocation and atomic counting. The book's chapter 10 repeats the idea with different absolute numbers (21.0, 44.2 and 22.3 ns, recorded in the no-evidence file) so absolute figures vary between runs or machines. First-party, CPU not stated. Tier C. Files opened: Chapter06/07_smartptr.C, 07_smartptr.h, 07_smartptr_ext.C.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: CRTP static polymorphism instead of virtual calls (chapter 8)
baseline: virtual member function call through a base-class pointer
workload: Google Benchmark, 32 repeated calls per iteration of a trivial member f(int) that adds to a member counter: through a base pointer to a virtual function (BM_dynamic), through a CRTP base (BM_static, BM_static1) and a plain non-virtual class (BM_none).
claimed_speedup: Book (relayed via the seed lead from the book, not shown on any repo page I opened): per iteration of 32 calls, virtual call 9.04 ns against 1.55 ns for the CRTP call and 1.60 ns for the plain non-virtual call. About 5.8x (derived from the relayed numbers).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. No build line in the opened source file and the README lists no flags.
stars_or_usage: 137 stars; Packt companion repository of the book Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023)
tradeoffs: Static dispatch fixes the derived type at compile time: no heterogeneous containers of base pointers, no runtime selection, code duplication per derived class. CRTP also lets the compiler inline the call.
caveats: Per-call figures work out to about 0.28 ns for the virtual call and about 0.05 ns for the CRTP and non-virtual calls (derived), below one cycle for the inlined versions, so the compiler folded the 32 inlined additions and the gap measures inlining and loop folding as much as dispatch cost. Virtual dispatch gives runtime flexibility that the CRTP version cannot, so the comparison is not feature-equal. Compiler, flags and CPU not stated, first-party, one tiny function. Tier C. File opened: Chapter08/01_function_call.C.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: small_queue, a fixed-capacity circular-buffer queue with local storage
workload: Google Benchmark, per iteration 32 repetitions of: push 7 ints, then while not empty read front() (DoNotOptimize) and pop(); std::queue<int> against small_queue (a 16-int power-of-two ring buffer inside the object).
claimed_speedup: Book table (relayed via the seed lead from the book, not shown on any repo page I opened): std::queue<int> 472 ns per iteration (67.8M items/s) against small_queue 100 ns (319.9M items/s). About 4.7x (derived from the relayed numbers).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. No build line in the opened source file and the README lists no flags.
stars_or_usage: 137 stars; Packt companion repository of the book Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023)
tradeoffs: Fixed capacity of 16 ints inside the object (push returns false when full), no heap allocation, no growth, trivially small; std::queue<int> is unbounded and deque-backed. Useful only when the maximum depth is known and small.
caveats: The queue as written in this file looks functionally wrong (by reading the source, not compiled or run here): push() writes buf_[(++front_) & 15] while front() reads buf_[tail_ & 15], so front() returns the element pushed one step earlier (the first read is an uninitialised slot) and the last pushed element is never read; the benchmark only passes front() to DoNotOptimize and checks no values, so the timing does not catch it, but the 4.7x is measured on a container that is not yet a correct FIFO. The size check also lets a 17th element in. Bounded versus unbounded, so not a drop-in replacement. Book numbers, compiler, flags and CPU not stated, first-party. Tier C. File opened: Chapter10/08_small_queue.C.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: template ScopeGuard instead of a std::function-based guard (chapter 11)
baseline: ScopeGuard holding its cleanup in a std::function<void()> (the book's type-erased guard)
workload: Google Benchmark of a scope guard that deletes a pointer: template ScopeGuard (callable stored by value, no type erasure) against the std::function guard and against a hand-written explicit delete, in the null-pointer case (BM_nodelete) and the always-allocate case (BM_delete).
claimed_speedup: Book (relayed via the seed lead from the book, not shown on any repo page I opened): template guard 4.50 ns and 4.56 ns, matching explicit delete (4.48 and 4.54 ns); std::function guard 6.29 ns and 13.4 ns. About 1.4x and 2.9x (derived from the relayed numbers). The same BM_delete rows appear (as BM_delete_explicit 4.54, BM_delete_type_erased 13.4, BM_delete_template 4.56 ns) in the book's preface console sample.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. No build line in the opened source file and the README lists no flags.
stars_or_usage: 137 stars; Packt companion repository of the book Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023)
tradeoffs: The guard type depends on the callable's type (use auto or a factory function), so it cannot be stored or returned under one common type without type erasure; code is generated per lambda.
caveats: The baseline is the book's own std::function guard, not a library guard (Boost.ScopeExit, folly::ScopeGuard, std::experimental::scope_exit), which are template designs like the winner and were not benchmarked. The 13.4 ns std::function row contains the new/delete pair (about 4.5 ns, the explicit-delete row), so the guard overhead there is about 8.9 ns against about 0.02 ns for the template guard (derived from the relayed numbers). Compiler, flags and CPU not stated, first-party. Tier C. File opened: Chapter11/11_scopeguard_te_benchmark.C.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: type-erased ScopeGuard with a fixed inline buffer (chapter 11)
baseline: ScopeGuard holding its cleanup in a std::function<void()>
workload: Same Google Benchmark as the template ScopeGuard entry: ScopeGuardTypeErasedFast (16-byte inline buffer plus a function-pointer invoker) against the std::function guard, null-pointer and always-allocate cases, explicit delete as floor.
claimed_speedup: Book (relayed via the seed lead from the book, not shown on any repo page I opened): buffer-based guard 5.48 ns against 6.29 ns for the std::function guard, and 12.7 ns against 13.4 ns when always allocating; explicit delete 4.48 and 4.54 ns. About 1.15x and 1.06x (derived from the relayed numbers).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. No build line in the opened source file and the README lists no flags.
stars_or_usage: 137 stars; Packt companion repository of the book Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023)
tradeoffs: Accepts only trivially copyable and trivially destructible callables up to 16 bytes (static_assert); no heap fallback.
caveats: Marginal gain (6 to 15%). By reading the source (not compiled or run here), ScopeGuardTypeErasedFast declares its own 'mutable bool commit_' that shadows CommitFlag::commit_, so commit() (which sets the base flag) does not suppress the cleanup and a moved-from guard still fires: the fast guard is not behaviourally equivalent to the std::function guard, and the benchmark never calls commit() so the timing does not show it. Baseline is the book's own std::function guard, not a library guard. Compiler, flags and CPU not stated, first-party. Tier C. File opened: Chapter11/11_scopeguard_te_benchmark.C.
